newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin enjoys modest electoral success.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin enjoys modest electoral success.

text.p: The Kremlin enjoyed some modest electoral success at the weekend when its candidates won three of seven elections for Russian regional governors, halting a recent run of defeats.

But communists and nationalists each chalked up a narrow victory and the two remaining races ended inconclusively and will go to a run-off round, according to results published on Monday by Russian news agencies.

Elections are being held for governors of 52 of Russia's 89 regions over several months up to the end of the year. They are not only a test of the government's popularity but could also shift the balance of power in parliament.

A total of 30 regions have voted so far, electing 24 governors to sit in the Federation Council (upper house). In two regions a second round of elections will be held, and in four there will be a re-run.

The upper house has so far been dominated by regional leaders appointed by President Boris Yeltsin. Relatively few of this appointees have won reelection and the opposition says the overall tally is balanced between government and opposition.
In seven regional elections last month, only one Kremlin-backed candidate secured reelection.

The Kremlin, however, puts a more favourable spin on the results. An official said on Monday that 19 of all the governors elected supported the government line, while most of the remaining five were not hardline opponents and would opt for dialogue with Yeltsin's administration.
"They (the 19) directly and consistently follow the government course," said an aide to the Kremlin deputy chief-of-staff, Alexander Kazakov.

"Others can only be called opposition formally. When they start the campaign they criticise the government. When they become governors they become statesmen. They are getting farther from the opposition and closer to cooperation," he said.
One of the most colourful personalities elected so far is Alexander Rutskoi, chosen as governor of the central Kursk region last month.
Former vice-president to Yeltsin, in 1993 Rutskoi was jailed for several months after leading an uprising against the Kremlin leader, crushed by army tanks.
But he took a moderate line after his election, saying he wanted to forget old battles and stressing his eagerness to cooperate with the Kremlin for the benefit of his region.

In the races this weekend, Governor Konstantin Titov won in a runoff in the central Samara region against a communist rival. In Ivanovo, also in central Russia, local leader Vladislav Tikhomirov won a second term.
In the far eastern Kamchatka region, much closer to Japan than to Moscow, Kremlin-appointed Vladimir Biryukov won convincingly with 60 percent of the votes.
But Communist-backed Alexander Surikov won a narrow victory in a second round ballot in the south Siberian Altai region over Kremlin-backed Lev Korshunov.
In the Arctic port city of Murmansk, nationalist Yuri Yevdokimov, representing the Congress of Russian Communities, beat incumbent Yevgeny Komarov by a tight margin.
But there will be a second round of voting in the southern Siberian Khakassia region and in Nenets in the north.
